analysis.one_liner: Adds dental, vision, and hearing coverage to Medicare.
analysis.headline: The bill would make Medicare cover dental cleanings, crowns and dentures, eye exams and glasses, and hearing exams and hearing aids starting in 2026, but it has sat without action in two House committees since its March 2025 introduction despite 131 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill adds three benefits Medicare does not currently cover: dental care (cleanings, fillings, crowns, root canals, dentures, emergency dental work), vision care (eye exams, glasses, contacts), and hearing care (exams, hearing aids). Coverage starts January 1, 2026, with Medicare paying 100% of preventive dental care immediately and phasing in to 80% of most other services by 2029; low-income beneficiaries get the full 80% faster. It has been referred to two House committees and has not moved since.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 65 million people on Medicare — seniors and people with disabilities — who today pay out of pocket for dental, vision, and hearing care, all of which Medicare excludes. Dental problems and untreated hearing and vision loss are among the most common and costly unmet health needs of older Americans. Low-income beneficiaries gain the most, since the bill gives them the full coverage phase-in immediately. Dental, vision, and hearing providers also gain a new federal payer.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Seniors and disabled people on Medicare

how_it_helps.text: Medicare would cover routine dental cleanings and exams, basic and major dental services, emergency dental care, and dentures — services currently excluded from Medicare entirely.

Medicare would cover routine eye exams, eyeglass lenses and frames, contact lenses, and low vision devices, with a one-exam-per-year limit and dollar caps on eyewear ($100 for lenses, $100 for frames every two years, $200 for contacts every two years, adjusted for inflation).

Medicare would cover routine hearing exams and pay 80% of the cost of hearing aids, limited to one hearing aid per ear every 48 months — hearing aids today typically cost thousands of dollars out of pocket.

Low-income beneficiaries get full coverage faster: Medicare pays 100% of preventive dental care and 80% of other dental services for subsidy-eligible individuals starting in 2027, while other beneficiaries wait until 2029 for the 80% rate.
The bill repeals the statutory grounds that currently exclude dental, eyeglasses, and hearing aids from Medicare, and adds an oral health professional to the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers, through higher Medicare spending; the bill contains no taxes or offsets to pay for the new benefit, so the cost would add to the federal deficit unless funded separately. Beneficiaries also share the cost: after the phase-in, they pay the standard 20% Medicare coinsurance on most dental, vision, and hearing services, and face limits — eyewear capped at $100, one hearing aid per ear every four years, one set of dentures every five years, and the Secretary of Health and Human Services may impose prior authorization requirements.

drawbacks.text: The bill has no funding mechanism — no taxes, premium changes, or offsets — so the entire cost of the new benefit would fall on the federal budget and add to the deficit.
The help arrives slowly for most beneficiaries: Medicare pays 0% of non-preventive dental services before 2027, only 30% in 2027 and 60% in 2028, reaching 80% only in 2029.

The caps are tight relative to real-world prices: eyeglass lenses and frames are capped at $100 each, contacts at $200 every two years, dentures are limited to one set every five years, and hearing aids to one per ear every four years — and the Health and Human Services Secretary can add prior authorization and other limits on all three benefits.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This is a real, substantial benefit: dental, vision, and hearing care are three of the largest out-of-pocket health costs for older Americans, and untreated hearing loss and dental disease carry serious health consequences. The honest case against it is that it is an uncosted expansion — no offset means deficit-financed spending that will fuel pressure for cuts elsewhere — and that the design dilutes the benefit: multi-year phase-ins and low dollar caps mean limited help in the early years, exactly when budgets are tightest. A well-designed version would pair the coverage with funding and stronger caps.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in March 2025 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees, where it has sat ever since with no hearing, no markup, and no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Lloyd Doggett introduced the Medicare Dental, Vision, and Hearing Benefit Act on March 11, 2025, with 131 original cosponsors, all Democrats.
The bill was referred to two committees — Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means — for consideration of the provisions under each committee's jurisdiction.
The complete action history shows no further action: no committee markup, hearing, or floor vote has been scheduled in the months since introduction.

Congress remains in session until January 2027, so the bill could still move, but bills adding new Medicare benefits rarely advance as standalone measures without bipartisan support or attachment to a larger package.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No outcome has been reached, so no one has gained or lost yet. So far the status quo holds: Medicare still excludes dental, vision, and hearing care, and seniors continue paying out of pocket or buying private supplemental coverage for it.

sides.party_line_note: All 131 cosponsors are Democrats and none of the bill's supporters is Republican, so the bill's support is entirely one-party; no vote has occurred to confirm how the full chamber would split.

industries.note: Medicare would become a new federal payer for cleanings, fillings, crowns, root canals, and dentures, directing federal money to dental practices and making care affordable for seniors who currently skip it.

Hearing aids, which usually cost thousands of dollars out of pocket, would be covered at 80% with one per ear every four years — a large new market funded by Medicare, and the bill also exempts hearing aids from Medicare's competitive bidding program.
Routine eye exams and eyewear would get a Medicare payer, though the $100 lens and $100 frame caps and $200 contact limit are well below what many retailers charge, tempering the gain.

industries.industry: Private dental and vision insurance sellers
industries.note: Standalone dental and vision plans and supplemental coverage are sold largely because Medicare excludes these services; if Medicare covered them directly, a slice of that private market would disappear.

These insurers would have to include the new benefits in their basic package, raising their costs, while losing the marketing appeal of offering dental, vision, and hearing as extras that steer seniors into private plans.

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican cosponsors, no committee action five months after introduction, and the bill parked in two committees at once, the realistic path is that it sits until the Congress ends in January 2027 unless Democrats attach a version of it to a larger package they have the votes to pass — which they do not currently have in either chamber.
